text:
非官方数据推算：Bitget 这次被盗的 3.516 亿美元，大概相当于八个月利润

先说结论：

Bitget 的被盗事情出现后，我就把 Coinbase、Bybit 和 Bitget 的数据放到一起交叉计算，估算出 Bitget 目前一年的利润大概在 5.3 亿—5.5 亿美元，这次涉及的 3.516 亿美元，相当于全年利润的 64%—66%，换算下来大概就是 7.7—7.9 个月。

以上数据都是我个人的估算，不代表是官方数据。

以下是我推算的过程：

2025 年 Bybit 被盗约 14.6 亿美元，当时 Ben 公开表示，这笔钱大约相当于 Bybit 一年的利润。所以可以把 Bybit 在上一轮行情中的年利润先放在 14.6 亿—15 亿美元附近。

然后用 Coinbase 的公开财报调整一下现在的市场环境。

Coinbase 2024 年交易收入是 39.86 亿美元，到了 2026 年第二季度只剩 5.99 亿美元。按照第二季度年化，大概是 23.96 亿美元，相当于 2024 年的 60.1%。

也就是说，如果用 Coinbase 的收入变化代表交易所现在赚钱能力相对 2024 年的变化，那么 Bybit 当年的约 15 亿美元利润，放到现在大概还剩：

15 亿 × 60.1% = 9.02 亿美元

接下来再比较 Bybit 和 Bitget 现在的规模。

TokenInsight 统计，今年第二季度整个交易所市场成交量约 16.5 万亿美元。

Bybit 市占率 9.81%，对应成交量约 1.62 万亿美元。

Bitget 同期成交量约 9,840 亿美元，相当于 Bybit 的 60.8%。

两家的业务结构还比较接近，Bybit 第二季度约 75% 的成交量来自衍生品，Bitget约 79% 。

最后就是：

15 亿 × 60.1% × 60.8% ≈ 5.48 亿美元

如果按照 Bybit 实际被盗的 14.6 亿美元计算，则是：

14.6 亿 × 60.1% × 60.8% ≈ 5.33 亿美元

因此我姑且把 Bitget 目前的年利润暂时估在 5.3 亿—5.5 亿美元。

对应这次 3.516 亿美元的损失：

3.516 ÷ 5.48 = 64.2%

也就是大约 7.7 个月利润。

即便考虑两家手续费、返佣、营销成本和员工成本存在差异，给最终结果上下浮动 20%，Bitget 年利润大概也就是 4.3 亿—6.6 亿美元。这样计算，这次损失对应的利润时间大概在 6.4—9.8 个月。

所以目前用公开数据去推，我会把这次 Bitget 被盗理解成 损失了大约八个月利润，这个金额放到 Bitget 自己过去的市场投入里可以得出的结论：

Bitget 当年和 Messi 合作期间，曾经宣布投入 2,000 万美元做营销活动和用户奖励。这次损失的 3.516 亿美元，相当于 17.6 个这样的 2,000 万美元营销计划。

所以 3.516 亿美元用在 Bitget 自己过去几年的品牌投入里，已经是一个非常夸张的数字。

从这个角度来说，这次肯定不能算“小损失”。所以目前这个损失程度，我更愿意形容成，已经伤筋，但暂时还谈不上动骨。

希望 Bitget 可以安稳渡过这次事件，早日开放提款。这种对于交易所的攻击，说不定又是那谁谁谁了。

[SECURITY NOTICE] Bitget Hot Wallet Incident — September 24, 2026

At 18:31 UTC on September 24, 2026, Bitget's security systems detected unauthorized transfers from some of our hot wallets. Our security team activated emergency response protocols immediately.

What we have confirmed:
-Estimated funds affected: approximately $351.6 million
-Cold wallets remain fully secure. Bitget operates a three-tier wallet architecture — the breach contained only a portion of the hot wallet and warm wallet layers.
-User funds are safe. The full amount of this loss falls within the coverage of Bitget's User Protection Fund, which currently holds over $464 million

Actions we have taken:
-Emergency response team activated within minutes of detection
-Abnormal transfer addresses identified, flagged, and reported
-Withdrawals temporarily suspended as a precautionary measure, pending security review
-Law enforcement and on-chain security firms have been formally notified and are engaged

What this means for you:
-Your account balances are accurate and your assets are protected
-Deposits and trading remain fully operational
Withdrawals are temporarily paused and will be restored as soon as the security review is complete
-What comes next: We will provide updates on an hourly basis across this channel and all official platforms. A full incident report — including root cause analysis and corrective actions — will be published within 24 hours. We will not speculate on the attack vector until the investigation is complete.

Bitget has navigated multiple market cycles. We will not run from this. Every dollar and every decision will be accounted for, transparently and in full.
Updates will be posted here and across all official Bitget channels as they become available.

— Gracy Chen, CEO, Bitget

text:
One of the biggest questions I've been getting is: How can you have a perp on a startup if there is no external market price for that startup?

The answer is that the market becomes less like a perp and more like a prediction market, where the market will eventually converge to the external market price when one exists (e.g. when the startup IPOs or gets acquired or shuts down).

The convergence happens because funding rates push the perp market to match the external market price once it exists. If the perp price is trading below the public market price, shorts pay longs to encourage the price to move up. And vice versa when it's trading too high.

Before the external market price exists, the guarantee that this convergence will eventually happen is what drives the market to price itself accurately. Just like a prediction market.

In the past, perps have become popular as a means of trading private companies right before their IPOs, like SpaceX as one recent example. But where traditional perps fail is when the convergence event is far in the future or uncertain, like it is for the vast majority of private companies.

Even very large private companies such as Stripe and Anduril, which are very popular, are not currently accessible by modern perp implementations used by Binance and Hyperliquid. This is because their risk management systems cannot handle the lower liquidity of such markets, and their market-makers are not equipped to provide the necessary liquidity to get them over the threshold.

Specifically, if a traditional perp has a large price gap and results in a lot of users going negative, the exchange has historically been on the hook for that bad debt. The risk to the exchange of paying down massive insolvencies on illiquid markets has thus prevented major exchanges from listing markets unless they have relatively high liquidity on day one.

MicroPerps can solve this by eliminating the risk to the exchange of listing highly-illiquid perps, essentially solving the liquidity chicken-and-egg. Instead of requiring massive liquidity on day one in order for a perp to be viable, a MicroPerp can simply exist until just the right moment when users and market-makers deem it to be worth their time to trade.

As such, the true advantage of a MicroPerp is that it allows the exchange to be "first to list" for all assets of interest, making it the focal point of trading when interest and liquidity eventually do come to meet the threshold.

text:
🚨 Jeff Yan’s Bitget Warning Is Back in the Spotlight

After Bitget’s reported ~$351.6M security incident, an old warning from Hyperliquid co-founder Jeff Yan is getting renewed attention.

Yan previously criticized Bitget’s trading structure, alleging that the exchange could benefit from taking the other side of user flow and raising concerns around conflicts of interest.

His broader argument was simple:
When an exchange controls the venue, custody and trading exposure, users have to trust the platform instead of being able to independently verify the system.

That’s where @HyperliquidX takes a very different approach.

Hyperliquid is built around an on-chain trading infrastructure where positions, liquidations and market activity can be independently observed on-chain.

The contrast matters.

FTX showed the danger of trusting an opaque exchange with too many interconnected roles. Bitget’s latest incident is a reminder that custody and exchange infrastructure remain major points of failure in crypto.

To be clear, the current Bitget incident does not prove Yan’s previous allegations or establish that Bitget is insolvent.

But it does bring the same question back:
How much of an exchange’s risk can users actually verify for themselves?

That transparency is one of the core ideas behind Hyperliquid’s onchain model.

text:
In February 2025, Bybit lost $1.5B in the biggest hack crypto has ever seen.

Within a day, Bitget sent over 40,000 ETH to help it keep withdrawals running. It didn't need to. Bybit is its competitor. Bybit paid it back within days, and no user lost a dollar.

What goes around comes around, they say.
1.5 years later, the roles are reversed.

Bitget lost $351M yesterday, and Bybit is the first one offering to help. It's updating LazarusBounty, the tracker it built after its own hack, to follow where Bitget's stolen funds go. Bitget believes Lazarus is behind this one too.

This is the part of crypto we should keep working on: coordinating the response when these groups strike.

Attackers work as organized groups. Over $684M has been stolen this September alone, and every hack teaches them something new.

The industry only works if we defend it the same way.

Respect to Ben and the Bybit team.

author: PhyrexNi
quoted_text:
非官方数据推算：Bitget 这次被盗的 3.516 亿美元，大概相当于八个月利润

先说结论：

Bitget 的被盗事情出现后，我就把 Coinbase、Bybit 和 Bitget 的数据放到一起交叉计算，估算出 Bitget 目前一年的利润大概在 5.3 亿—5.5 亿美元，这次涉及的 3.516 亿美元，相当于全年利润的 64%—66%，换算下来大概就是 7.7—7.9 个月。

以上数据都是我个人的估算，不代表是官方数据。

以下是我推算的过程：

2025 年 Bybit 被盗约 14.6 亿美元，当时 Ben 公开表示，这笔钱大约相当于 Bybit 一年的利润。所以可以把 Bybit 在上一轮行情中的年利润先放在 14.6 亿—15 亿美元附近。

然后用 Coinbase 的公开财报调整一下现在的市场环境。

Coinbase 2024 年交易收入是 39.86 亿美元，到了 2026 年第二季度只剩 5.99 亿美元。按照第二季度年化，大概是 23.96 亿美元，相当于 2024 年的 60.1%。

也就是说，如果用 Coinbase 的收入变化代表交易所现在赚钱能力相对 2024 年的变化，那么 Bybit 当年的约 15 亿美元利润，放到现在大概还剩：

15 亿 × 60.1% = 9.02 亿美元

接下来再比较 Bybit 和 Bitget 现在的规模。

TokenInsight 统计，今年第二季度整个交易所市场成交量约 16.5 万亿美元。

Bybit 市占率 9.81%，对应成交量约 1.62 万亿美元。

Bitget 同期成交量约 9,840 亿美元，相当于 Bybit 的 60.8%。

两家的业务结构还比较接近，Bybit 第二季度约 75% 的成交量来自衍生品，Bitget约 79% 。

最后就是：

15 亿 × 60.1% × 60.8% ≈ 5.48 亿美元

如果按照 Bybit 实际被盗的 14.6 亿美元计算，则是：

14.6 亿 × 60.1% × 60.8% ≈ 5.33 亿美元

因此我姑且把 Bitget 目前的年利润暂时估在 5.3 亿—5.5 亿美元。

对应这次 3.516 亿美元的损失：

3.516 ÷ 5.48 = 64.2%

也就是大约 7.7 个月利润。

即便考虑两家手续费、返佣、营销成本和员工成本存在差异，给最终结果上下浮动 20%，Bitget 年利润大概也就是 4.3 亿—6.6 亿美元。这样计算，这次损失对应的利润时间大概在 6.4—9.8 个月。

所以目前用公开数据去推，我会把这次 Bitget 被盗理解成 损失了大约八个月利润，这个金额放到 Bitget 自己过去的市场投入里可以得出的结论：

Bitget 当年和 Messi 合作期间，曾经宣布投入 2,000 万美元做营销活动和用户奖励。这次损失的 3.516 亿美元，相当于 17.6 个这样的 2,000 万美元营销计划。

所以 3.516 亿美元用在 Bitget 自己过去几年的品牌投入里，已经是一个非常夸张的数字。

从这个角度来说，这次肯定不能算“小损失”。所以目前这个损失程度，我更愿意形容成，已经伤筋，但暂时还谈不上动骨。

希望 Bitget 可以安稳渡过这次事件，早日开放提款。这种对于交易所的攻击，说不定又是那谁谁谁了。

text:
It hardly makes any sense.

Vaults in Morpho exist to solve a UX problem, as users simply cannot track thousands of markets themselves. But vaults do not offer much additional protection to users. In fact, they significantly reduce user protection compared to depositing directly into a market.

The absolute majority of users will not understand what changes are being introduced under a 1-day timelock, even if they somehow decide to monitor the vault 24/7. And the existence of a timelock does not mean that every investment decision made by the curator is implicitly approved by the lender.

Coming back to the first point, Paul says that “the vault turns the complexity of tracking thousands of markets into a single set of predetermined rules that allocates across many markets at once.” But now the user effectively has to monitor the thousands of markets the curator allocates to. And if the funds are mismanaged, we can suddenly say that this was done with the user's “explicit or implicit” approval.

And I am not even talking about situations where curators use their “discretionary” vaults as collateral within their non-custodial vaults. What is the vault called in that situation?

I do not think Paul is naive enough to believe that these vaults are “non-custodial”. Rather, he seems to want others to believe in that.

[SECURITY NOTICE] Bitget Hot Wallet Incident — September 24, 2026

At 18:31 UTC on September 24, 2026, Bitget's security systems detected unauthorized transfers from some of our hot wallets. Our security team activated emergency response protocols immediately.

What we have confirmed:
-Estimated funds affected: approximately $351.6 million
-Cold wallets remain fully secure. Bitget operates a three-tier wallet architecture — the breach contained only a portion of the hot wallet and warm wallet layers.
-User funds are safe. The full amount of this loss falls within the coverage of Bitget's User Protection Fund, which currently holds over $464 million

Actions we have taken:
-Emergency response team activated within minutes of detection
-Abnormal transfer addresses identified, flagged, and reported
-Withdrawals temporarily suspended as a precautionary measure, pending security review
-Law enforcement and on-chain security firms have been formally notified and are engaged

What this means for you:
-Your account balances are accurate and your assets are protected
-Deposits and trading remain fully operational
Withdrawals are temporarily paused and will be restored as soon as the security review is complete
-What comes next: We will provide updates on an hourly basis across this channel and all official platforms. A full incident report — including root cause analysis and corrective actions — will be published within 24 hours. We will not speculate on the attack vector until the investigation is complete.

Bitget has navigated multiple market cycles. We will not run from this. Every dollar and every decision will be accounted for, transparently and in full.
Updates will be posted here and across all official Bitget channels as they become available.

— Gracy Chen, CEO, Bitget

THORChain and Stolen Funds: The Industry Needs Answers

After the $1.46B @Bybit_Official hack last year, nearly $1.2B in stolen funds was reportedly traced through @THORChain as the attackers moved assets across chains.

Today, following another major security incident at @Bitget , we are once again observing Bitget Exploiter funds being sent into the THORChain for asset swaps and cross-chain transfers.

The question is no longer:

“Does THORChain know these funds are associated with hackers?”

The attacker addresses have already been publicly flagged and are being actively tracked by exchanges, blockchain security/aml firms, and the wider crypto industry.

The real question is:

When a protocol is aware that funds originate from a publicly identified major hack, yet continues to facilitate large-scale cross-chain swaps, how should the industry view this under the banner of “decentralization”?

Decentralization should not become a blanket excuse when dealing with known stolen funds.

If, after every major crypto hack, attackers can continue using THORChain as a route to move funds from ETH → BTC, BNB → BTC, and across other chains, the industry needs to seriously ask:

What responsibility should THORChain bear when handling known stolen funds?

text: Somehow, I happen to work on both Quick Slots prototype and its spec. A prototype discovers hidden complications while a spec makes the intended behavior explicit. Although neither means we should do it, the spec gives the community something concrete to discuss. Hope this week I spent on it leads us to a more informed decision.
author: barnabemonnot
quoted_text:
Happy to report that after a month of work, EIP-8198 aka Quick Slots was merged as a feature spec in the Ethereum consensus specs! Many thanks to @jih2nn and @JustinTraglia for their tireless work as spec maintainers  🙌

What does "merging specifications" mean? Specifying a feature means writing up its behaviour, in code and in English, in a repository that has accumulated the detailed description of every feature since the launch of Ethereum’s Proof-of-Stake chain. This is the ground truth of how Ethereum consensus runs, and the model that all consensus clients follow to come to agreement with each other.

Anyone can contribute to this repository, by submitting “pull requests” with more code and more text specifying a new feature. Pull requests remain open while the proposed changes and additions are reviewed, by specs maintainers and by the persons submitting their contributions. Once they have been sufficiently reviewed, with edge cases uncovered, the pull request can then be “merged”, and live inside the codebase of the specs, instead of besides it.

This is usually a signal that the feature’s specs are now stable enough to evaluate in the context of other proposed changes. In particular, it also makes it easier for clients who want to start prototyping the feature, to do so on specifications that are no longer expected to change drastically. There can still be misses and unknowns, but at least the current thing has passed this first, close review.

Importantly, this does not mean that faster slots have made it into Hegotá. We are still two steps away from it: Quick slots were Proposed for Inclusion on August 6th, and next week, on October 1st, we will likely be discussing raising its level to Considered for Inclusion at ACD. Should a decision then be made to include in the fork, quick slots would then become Scheduled for Inclusion, the last step. PFI -> CFI -> SFI. Easy eh? 😅

So this means the job's not done 🫡 We'll continue to advocate for a strong prototype of quick slots based on the specifications. We're continuing our outreach to ecosystem smart contracts and teams for who a slot change may impact their operations. And we're continuing to research the future of shortening slot times with post-quantum cryptography and zkEVM in view, beyond Hegotá.

In the meantime, find the specs here: https://t.co/H1tgsmB0yv

text:
The Disclosure Gap in Morpho Vaults

Every curator change is public onchain, but few depositors can read it. The timelock meant to protect them only works if they notice in time.

1. Common critique 1: Timelock is not an enough safeguard
A common critique goes further. Vaults were meant to save users from tracking thousands of markets, and a 1-day timelock hands that job straight back while treating the user's silence as approval.

I agree that silence during a timelock isn't consent. Most depositors couldn't interpret a cap increase or an oracle swap even if they watched the vault around the clock. Where I disagree is the claim that vaults themselves are the problem.

2. Common critique 2: Mandate Drift
Mandate drift is the biggest risk on that list. A depositor who picks a vault built on blue-chip collateral hasn't agreed to whatever the curator adds a year later. In TradFi, a change to a fund's fundamental investment policy needs a shareholder vote.

A competent risk rating provider can flag drift onchain if two conditions hold. The vault has to publish a mandate to measure against, and the rating has to update the moment a change is proposed, while depositors can still exit.

3. Common critique 3: Roles
Role separation mainly protects against compromised keys, because an allocator can only move funds within existing caps and can't add new markets.

It protects depositors only when independent parties hold the roles. When one team holds every role, the split tells you who to blame after a loss and does little else.

4. Curators as asset managers

Curators ARE asset managers, and they abstract markets away from the user the way an ETF abstracts away its holdings. Nobody buying an S&P 500 ETF monitors 500 companies.

A bad ETF issuer makes investing riskier than picking stocks yourself, and a good one diversifies away risk most people couldn't manage alone. You can diversify on your own, yet US ETFs passed $10T in assets in 2024 because most people would rather not.

5. What ETFs disclose

ETFs earned that trust through the disclosure rules around them. A US fund that wants to raise its advisory fee or change its adviser needs a shareholder vote. A fund that changes a name tied to its investment policy owes investors 60 days' notice. ETFs also publish their holdings daily.

Cuts to cost or risk take effect immediately, while increases need notice or consent. Morpho already encodes that asymmetry onchain: cap increases and other risk-increasing changes sit behind a timelock, and cap decreases don't.

6. The missing layer

What's missing is interpretation. The Morpho app shows pending changes, but as raw parameters that only a DeFi native can read.

A depositor should be able to subscribe to a vault and get a plain-language alert when any of these change:

• Oracles
• Timelock length
• Roles: owner, curator, allocators, and any abdicated functions
• Collateral whitelist
• Performance and management fees
• Vault name
• Market caps
• New adapters
• Market allocation

Each alert should state how the change moves the vault's risk and how much liquidity is free to exit before it executes, since a 7-day timelock protects nobody when the underlying markets sit at 100% utilisation.

7. Who should report

Curators can't do this reporting themselves, since they have a conflict of interest when reporting on their own vaults. Morpho benefits from vault growth, so it isn't fully neutral either.

Integrators could take the broker role that exists in TradFi, or a rating firm like Credora could, provided the curators it rates aren't paying for the ratings.

8. Steakhouse as the benchmark

@SteakhouseFi comes closest today. Its vaults carry @CredoraNetwork risk ratings with a published methodology, and its guardian is an @AragonProject DAO where depositors vote with their vault shares.

Changes sit behind a 7-day timelock, anyone holding around $10K of shares can propose a revocation, and the vote runs for one day. That makes it the nearest thing DeFi has to a shareholder vote. The veto still depends on depositors knowing a change is pending, so it needs the alerting layer to work.

9. What should come next
Vaults is a great technology. What they need next is notice that depositors can read and act on. That requires alerts + interpretation, not just instant event level notification. No investors would understand it.

text:
A year into FXRP, we’re getting a sneak peek at what @FlareNetworks could become, does Flare’s infrastructure truly turn $XRP into a future-proof asset?

But we’re going beyond the basics to delve further.

In crypto, you’re usually forced to spin up wallets, hop across bridges, and scrounge up gas tokens just to get moving.

Flare has spent the past year cutting that obstacle course down to size, and it begins with two built-in tools:

- FTSO supplies prices, while FDC verifies outside events, including XRP payments. Flare’s validators also secure these data protocols, giving its products a shared foundation.

- FAssets turns XRP into FXRP for use in DeFi. Minting requires proof of the XRP payment. Redemption agents operate under collateral, challenge and liquidation rules.

The Core Vault holds pooled XRP under a Flare-governed multisig, with escrow time locks and withdrawal controls. Agents cannot simply walk away with it.

Flare Smart Accounts make access incredibly simple.

Sign an XRPL transaction from your current wallet. FDC verifies it, and your linked smart account executes on Flare. The vault flow now needs one signature, no separate EVM key or gas token.

By July, Flare reported nearly 24,000 smart accounts and FXRP in DeFi growing from 82 million in February to 144 million.

So, what's next? It is Flare Confidential Compute (FCC)

FCC is a verifiable computation that keeps sensitive data private, plus protocol-managed wallets that can act on other chains. Songbird first, with broader deployment still ahead.

Finally, how all these changes benefits $FLR.

FIP.16 cuts annual inflation from 5% to 3%. Transaction fees burn, while FIRE collects specified protocol fees, with supply reduction as its first mandate alongside other governed uses.

---

What keeps me upbeat about Flare is how coherently the pieces fit together.

FXRP expands what XRP can do, Smart Accounts remove friction for users, and confidential compute opens the door to privacy sensitive apps, while the value flow ultimately routes back to FLR.

None of this is starting from zero. Each layer builds on real progress already in place, which makes the Flare faces almost competition and more scalable.

That said, activity still has to mature into real, durable revenue over time.

Still, after a year of FXRP, there is a functioning baseline, something concrete to iterate on, and a clearer runway toward wider adoption.

You are still not bullish enough.

既然ZEC是隐私币，为什么每次黑客都还是会把资金转换成ETH？昨天在Bitget被盗后很多朋友都提出了这个问题，确实几乎所有能历数的大型黑客事件，被盗的稳定币、山寨币都会被快速转成ETH，其实原因非常简单，顺着我的逻辑往下看
1.对于黑客来说，相比于隐私，安全更重要，一定要确保自己辛辛苦苦盗走的钱不会被冻结，而绝大多数稳定币、山寨币都有黑名单，大部分公链也都可以节点回滚，所以黑客必须第一时间快速把盗走的资金转换为不可被冻结的资产。
2.这时候你会问，那BTC也不会被回滚，更没有黑名单，为什么不换成BTC呢？答案是当然会换，但是要慢慢换，因为黑客在链上和交易所里盗走的绝大多数资产都是在以太坊主网上的，当然是直接换成ETH速度最快，不需要等着跨链，这时候必须要拼手速，否则慢悠悠的等跨完早都被冻结了，所以ZEC等其他的隐私币也是同样的道理。
3.刚才说到相比于隐私，安全更重要，所以快速换成ETH确保安全后，黑客才会高枕无忧，接下来十几天甚至几个月，慢悠悠的把ETH拆成几千上万个地址，然后用THORChain这些洗币桥和混币器慢慢的换成BTC。
4.然后经过长达几年的时间，大量小额分批掉通过场外和地下钱庄把BTC兑现。
所以隐私不隐私的，黑客根本不在意的好伐，人家有太多手段把钱洗出去。
当然黑客喜欢用ETH的原因还有一个，就是人家朝鲜是真的办过平壤以太坊大会啊🤣

quoted_text:
So bullish onchain options I’m getting palpitations. I think they’re the biggest missing unlock in the onchain asset stack.

We’re building spot liquidity, borrow markets and distribution around the same assets. The constraint running through all three is who’s willing to warehouse the risk, at what price, and for how long.

LPs already carry inventory risk. Holders want yield. Traders want convexity. Options create a market between those needs: holders can sell upside, traders can buy exposure or protection, and dealers can hedge inventory.

That can change the economics of supporting an asset onchain. More risk capacity can support better execution; better execution makes larger positions and lending markets more viable; distribution can package those capabilities into products people actually want to hold.

Attracting deposits into an options yield product is only half the equation, though. That yield comes from traders paying for exposure or hedgers paying for protection. The market becomes sustainable when those buyers keep coming back because the product is useful. Get that right and options can support durable demand across the entire market around an asset.

text:
At 9AM EST today somebody abused a bug in Payment Processor V2 to steal 10 Meebits, 50 Otherdeeds, 10 WoW, and 235 Desperate Apewives.

It wasn't until over 12 hours later that somebody reported it to me, and upon digging in I realized that a great many NFTs were subject to the same exploit.

I got in touch with the team over at LimitBreak and they quickly paused Payment Processor V3, which was subject to the same exploit. Unfortunately, V2 was not pausable, so the only path towards protecting affected assets was to run a whitehat operation.

Similarly, V3 on ApeChain is temporarily in a state where it cannot be paused, so ApeChain assets approved to V3 needed to be saved as well.

All in all, we rescued 23,155 NFTs worth north of $5.7M USD.

We later discovered that a similar exploit could be used in reverse to steal WETH. 660 WETH was at risk, which we unfortunately were not fast enough to recover. Apologies to those affected.

Shout out to @Boomskite for flagging the initial exploit tx to me, and @coffeedev @0xjustadev and @whiteoakkong for acting quickly and assisting with the recovery.

All NFTs are safely relocated. Soon, owners will be able claim them back after revoking the exploitable approvals.

Addresses to revoke below.

SoftBank just sold $11B of junk bonds at up to 9.75%. Largest high-yield sale on record, to fund the final $10B  tranche of its OpenAI commitment.

~10% debt funding an illiquid, zero-yield private stake! SoftBank borrowed against Arm and OpenAI shares: ~3/4 of its assets.

OpenAI itself projects $278B of negative free cash flow through 2030. Its $122B March raise runs out around 2028, leaving a ~$150B+ gap.

SoftBank can't lead the next round; it's paying junk yields to finish this one. And Anthropic may IPO first, competing for the same investors.

The part people miss: that $278B is only OpenAI's own gap. Oracle, SB Energy and neoclouds are borrowing against OpenAI's contracts to build the data centers. The total debt tied to OpenAI's revenue is far larger.

author: DeFiTeddy2020
quoted_text:
《交易所被盗后，散户该怎么做｜顺带看清“保险金”到底保什么》

交易所被黑，最慌的往往不是交易所，而是散户。

以 Bitget 此次热钱包事件为例。9 月 24 日，Bitget 公告称部分热钱包发生未经授权的资产转出，预计涉及约 3.516 亿美元。

虽然Bitget表示其超过 4.64 亿美元的用户保护基金足以覆盖此次损失，大家也要注意以下几点👇

1️⃣记住两件事情
1. 只认官网和已验证官方账号。任何“补偿领取、加急提币、客服链接”，一律按钓鱼处理。

2. 若提币未恢复，不要再入金，也不要加杠杆或抄底平台币。

2️⃣看清楚交易所说的保险到底保什么
交易所宣传的“保险”，可能并不是同一种东西：

1. 用户保护基金 / SAFU：平台被盗、系统级事故时，交易所拿出的应急池。多数是平台自有资金，按条款酌情赔付，不是银行存款保险。

2. 合约保险基金：只补合约强平穿仓，降低 ADL。不赔你现货被黑客转走。

3. 针对个人账号的保险：不是所有交易所、所有地区都有。建议查看所在交易所、所在地区的账户保险说明。

4. 储备金证明（PoR）：只说明某一时刻资产是否盖过用户负债，不是赔付承诺。

3️⃣各所保护基金公开机制
@Bitget：保护基金约 5500 BTC、官方称超 4.64 亿美元，地址可核验。本次缺口约 3.516 亿，官方称评估后由基金承担再补充。这是目前最直接对上“所被盗”的池子。
@Binance SAFU：约 1.5 万 BTC，目标约 12 亿美元；市值跌破约 8 亿承诺回补。
@OKX：Shield+Security Fund。Security Fund = 合约穿仓缓冲垫；Shield = 欧洲用户被盗号的酌情补偿（最高约 10 万–50 万欧元）。
@Coinbase：最高3.2亿美元，商业犯罪险，集团客户共享。含Custody、Prime，来自2026年年8月基金监管披露。
@HashKeyGroup ：香港持牌所走的是监管要求下的第三方托管保险，不是 Binance/Bitget 那种自建保护基金。公开口径包括热钱包高保额、冷钱包部分承保（集团 2025 年续保时称覆盖托管资产至少约 50%）。

4️⃣如何判断交易所是否会真金白银赔付
1. 有没有写明覆盖平台被黑客盗走用户资产，金额是否高于缺口、能否链上核验。

2. 提币何时恢复、恢复后是否卡审、限额、排队。

3. 历史上类似情形的赔付情况，大部分有承担的交易所都会赔偿，例如Binance 2019，Bybit 2025，但门头沟事件的破产清算拖了十余年，到现在还没有赔完。

5️⃣散户如何安放加密货币
1. 头部持牌的交易所，例如币安、coinbase和hashkey；
2. 如果具备管理硬件钱包的能力，推荐用硬件钱包存放大部分资金；
3. 做好资金分散，鸡蛋不要放在一个篮子里。不同交易所、冷钱包、热钱包分散管理。

🧐Bitget CEO：目前主要集中于安全修复，确认系统安全后将第一时间恢复提币

Bitget 首席执行官 @GracyBitget  于直播中表示，目前平台正在为恢复提币做准备，但尚无准确的恢复时间。

author: taodotcom
quoted_text:
This month, three of the biggest names in security all moved on the same problem at once. That does not happen by accident.

CrowdStrike shipped a product to secure AI agents at runtime. Proofpoint and Tenable each launched their own tools to inspect and control what agents are allowed to do. A startup built around AI red teaming got acquired.

That is a category being born in real time.

Agents did not fit the old security lanes. Endpoint, network, cloud, identity, none of them were built for something that reads, decides, and acts on its own across everything a company owns. So the industry is building a new lane for it, all at once, this month.

Even CrowdStrike's CEO put it plainly. Governance alone cannot stop an agent already in motion.

That is the whole point. You cannot write a policy and hope. You need a live layer that watches what the agent actually does and steps in before it acts. Control, not paperwork.

We did not need this week to tell us that. We have been building that exact layer for months.

Here is what the industry has not solved. Every one of those new products is owned by one company, a single vendor's closed box deciding what your agents can do. That is the same concentration of control we have been warning about all along.

The category is real and it is here. The only question left is whether the layer that governs every agent should belong to one company, or to a network that no one owns.

We already made our choice. Built on Bittensor, in the open, owned by no one.

The market just confirmed the problem. We are building the answer you do not have to take on trust.

text:
Memory Attention is a clever new twist on how Transformers build value vectors: instead of a big matrix multiply, it just looks up a token-specific memory and adds it to the contextual key—no extra compute, no loss of context.

What’s wild? This approach:
– Lowers perplexity (WikiText-103: 31.55→28.64) and boosts downstream accuracy (+0.6 to +1.2 points), using the *same* number of training tokens
– Makes training 1.16–1.42× more token-efficient
– Lets you stash giant memory tables off-GPU (even on CPU/SSD), freeing up GPU RAM by 7% while keeping latency flat
– Cuts value-path FLOPs by ~3%
– Holds 2.08× more parameters with no GPU memory blowup

And, it actually improves in-context recall—even beyond the model’s training window.

Takeaway: swapping a dense projection for a lookup and add not only speeds up inference and cuts resource use, but *improves* model quality. Opens the door to much larger, smarter LMs running on commodity hardware.

Get the full analysis here: https://t.co/FRYyBWuYxL

text:
Bittensor ($TAO) has one of the more interesting AI infrastructure stories in crypto

@chutes_ai, one of its largest AI inference subnets, offers inference at prices well below centralized providers

but @PineAnalytics found an interesting problem:

Chutes was estimated to generate only around $1.3–$2.4M/year in external customer revenue, while receiving roughly $52M/year in $TAO emissions based on Pine’s March 2026 snapshot

that’s roughly 22–40x more in network emissions than customer revenue

pine estimates that without those emissions, Chutes would need to charge around $1.41 per million tokens to cover the implied cost — compared with roughly $0.88/M for Llama 70B on Together AI

chutes is an interesting example of the bigger question in this machine economy thesis:

if customers keep paying for the service as incentives fall, that strengthens the case for genuine demand

if usage falls sharply when subsidies fall, then the headline usage numbers tell a very different story

useful work needs to pay its own bills

I run a grants programme that gives away smart contract audits.

Last season, eight protocols applied. Eight got funded. There were no rejections — not one.

Here is why that happened, and why Season 2 is open until October 4.

—

Why the programme exists

Almost every early-stage founder I talk to makes the same trade. A serious audit costs more than the runway allows. So they ship unaudited and hope, or they don't ship at all.

I've watched good protocols take that bet. I've watched some of them lose it.

That trade is the thing I'm trying to break. Not with a discount code — with real money against real engagements.

—

What actually happened in Season 1

Eight protocols applied, across six chains and four continents, with zero paid distribution. Not one was VC-funded. That's the number I'm proudest of.

We published the Builder tier at 25%. Then I read the applications: frozen commit hashes, honest line counts, real invariant suites. One team's mutation testing proved their own tests could fail. That isn't a pitch deck, that's engineering.

So we upgraded every Builder Grant to 50%. One time, in return for the trust those teams placed in a first-season programme.

Every applicant got an individual decision with the reasons. No form letters.

—

The part founders get wrong

We score the scaffolding, not the flaws.

Your bugs are not held against you. Your bugs are the reason the grant exists. A rich bug surface on solid foundations is the ideal applicant, not a disqualification.

If you've been putting this off because you think your code isn't ready — that's exactly backwards. Wait until it's clean and you'll be applying for an audit you no longer need.

—

Season 2

One protocol gets its audit 100% covered. Two get 50%. Builder grants cover 25% for the rest of the round.

Over $100,000, subsidised against our standard rate of $6,000 per auditor per week. Same founder-led, senior-only audit our paying clients get. Every report publishes in full when the engagement completes.

Applications close October 4. Winners announced October 11.

author: EdgarsNemse
quoted_text:
Edgars Nemše is the new CEO of the GenLayer Foundation.

The GenLayer Foundation has appointed @EdgarsNemse, GenLayer co-founder and Chief Product Officer, as its CEO. He leaves his role at GenLayer Labs and joins the Foundation full-time.

The timing is deliberate. Until now the Foundation's job was to set things up: the legal structure, the token framework, the first institutional relationships and the capital to launch well. With the token launch and mainnet approaching, the job changes. The Foundation becomes an operating organization: it stewards the treasury, brings projects onto the network and supports them with engineers, grows the validator set, and establishes the network's governance. On GenLayer those are technical jobs, and they need a technical operator.

Edgars co-authored the GenLayer whitepaper and has led the product from first prototype to the current testnet. Before GenLayer he was CTO at StakeHound and worked on trading strategies at Millburn Ridgefield, an $8B quantitative fund.

The Foundation's leadership team: @driudor, who founded the Foundation and has led it since, becomes Chief Institutional Officer, leading capital, institutions and key partners. @raskovsky is Chief Ecosystem Officer, bringing companies and their products onto GenLayer and growing its community. Xavi Cabezas is Chief Marketing Officer, taking GenLayer and the projects building on it to market. GenLayer Labs, led by @kstellana, remains the protocol and product company, focused on mainnet.

The Foundation's focus under Edgars:

— Through launch. Deliver the token launch and the network's early operations well, and run the treasury responsibly and openly.

— Adoption. GenLayer's adoption will come from teams and companies integrating intelligent contracts into real products. The Foundation's job is to find them, fund them, and build alongside them.

— Handing the network to itself. The Foundation's own work, grants, treasury decisions and governance, should eventually run directly on GenLayer. The end state is DeepThought, the on-chain organization that takes over the Foundation's role. The Foundation is working to a four-year horizon for that handover, and the work starts now.

More on each of these as mainnet approaches.

At 9AM EST today somebody abused a bug in Payment Processor V2 to steal 10 Meebits, 50 Otherdeeds, 10 WoW, and 235 Desperate Apewives.

It wasn't until over 12 hours later that somebody reported it to me, and upon digging in I realized that a great many NFTs were subject to the same exploit.

I got in touch with the team over at LimitBreak and they quickly paused Payment Processor V3, which was subject to the same exploit. Unfortunately, V2 was not pausable, so the only path towards protecting affected assets was to run a whitehat operation.

Similarly, V3 on ApeChain is temporarily in a state where it cannot be paused, so ApeChain assets approved to V3 needed to be saved as well.

All in all, we rescued 23,155 NFTs worth north of $5.7M USD.

We later discovered that a similar exploit could be used in reverse to steal WETH. 660 WETH was at risk, which we unfortunately were not fast enough to recover. Apologies to those affected.

Shout out to @Boomskite for flagging the initial exploit tx to me, and @coffeedev @0xjustadev and @whiteoakkong for acting quickly and assisting with the recovery.

All NFTs are safely relocated. Soon, owners will be able claim them back after revoking the exploitable approvals.

text:
The @BTCdrivechains Beta just went live!

Alpha helped the team uncover some of the biggest issues early: block instability, wallet balance display failures, stalled block parsing, invalid mining shares.

Now that Beta is live, I wanted to dig into what they're actually testing under real conditions ↓

1️⃣ More Realistic Mining Environment

Alpha started at Bitcoin’s minimum mining difficulty, allowing a small number of early miners to produce blocks while the network was getting started.

Beta started at around 1 BILLION. And no, that isn’t an exaggeration. That’s the actual starting difficulty.

That creates a more realistic test of block production, pool reliability, and difficulty adjustment.

But because Beta’s mining power may be unstable at first, exchanges should wait for more blocks before confirming deposits.

2️⃣ The Withdrawal Market

Drivechain withdrawals can be grouped into bundles with up to 6,000 individual payments.

A bundle needs a work score of 13,150 miner ACKs within a 26,300-block window before funds return to L1.

That process can take months, creating room for fast-withdrawal providers.

They give users the L1 funds upfront, collect the bundle later, and charge for taking on the wait.

Beta lets us see what that service actually costs.

3️⃣ Miner-controlled Sidechain Launches

Miners vote on new sidechains through the blocks they produce.

Voting for an unused slot lasts 2,016 blocks (or two weeks). A proposal is rejected after 1,008 non-ACK blocks, meaning it needs support from just over half of the network’s mining power.

Seven sidechains are planned for launch, covering scaling, privacy, identity, asset issuance, prediction markets, quantum resistance, and atomic swaps.

The level of support each one receives may offer an early signal of where miners see demand and fee opportunities (although their votes won’t measure either perfectly).

4️⃣ There is a retention problem

@DefiLlama currently tracks around $4.56B in TVL across 36 active Bitcoin protocols.

But its 2025 report showed a tougher picture for Bitcoin-aligned execution layers:

→ @Coredao_Org fell from $803.5M to $45.9M, a 94% drop
→ @BitlayerLabs dropped from $358.8M to $6.4M, a 98% drop
→ @rootstock_io held $153M by early December 2025, down 30.51% YoY

So for @BTCdrivechains, getting people to come back matters much more than the initial deposits.

On top of that, its sidechains need useful apps, dependable liquidity, and a simple way to move between L1 and L2.

5️⃣ Exchange Testing

eCash is built on Bitcoin Core v31.1, so exchanges can reuse much of their existing Bitcoin setup.

They still need separate nodes, accounting, and stronger deposit checks while the network stabilizes.

Beta gives them a chance to test all of this ahead of the mainnet launch targeted for October 31.

6️⃣ What comes next

I’ll mostly be watching repeat usage.

That means consistent payments to miners for sidechain commitments, enough liquidity to support fast withdrawals, and users returning to apps.

Those are the signals that Beta is moving towards real adoption.

Any dev curious about https://t.co/rdDSwFk6Td should probably jump into Beta now, build something, and tell the team what works and what breaks.

I found a new pattern that I'm getting a lot of value out of sharing because it might help other folks as well.

Let's say that you've created something pretty intense. I'm talking 12 days of 996 and it's validated to work.

How the hell do you uplift your team and teach them about the concepts? Before AI, we would start with a HLDD. After AI, I am increasingly finding that the HLDD comes afterwards.  HLDD's remain gold, you still need em but it's different now.
 
The pattern is simple. You have pre-commit hooks and skills that force the agent to automatically update the HLDD, and you self-host the HLDD in the application as documentation.

So, top of fold is still the human crafted why, measurement of success and how it will be measured. Below the fold is the how. 

But there's no reason why you can't intermix your personal remarks and your intent as editor remarks on each individual subsection.

Try it. It is very lit.

Let me let you guys in on a little secret...

I made a full-length brand trailer with Claude Opus 5.5 + ChatGPT Images 2.5 + Seedance 2.5 in Dreamfort today... 

and you can too! 

The future is already here:
- I no longer need to spend hours prompting video models to generate a single scene.
- Opus 5.5 can act as a director and can prompt these models in a great way for me.
- I just give it notes, the way a director gives notes to a crew.

My exact workflow:
- Opus 5.5 acts as the director agent.
- I first make a storyboard with Opus once I've sparred with it and finalized a plot.
- Each scene in the storyboard is represented as a series of clips.
- For each clip, I ask Opus to generate multiple reference images with ChatGPT Images 2.5: the first frame, the last frame, and a sheet for every character in it.
- I give each character a name. Opus then ensures that each character is consistent across every scene.
- Opus writes a timed Seedance 2.5 prompt for every clip: what each image is for, what happens second by second, every line of dialogue, every sound.
- It even drives DreamFort in Chrome for me: uploads the frames, pastes the prompts, renders each clip.
- Then it watches every take frame by frame and transcribes every line. When a shot is wrong, it redraws the keyframe instead of rewriting the prompt.
- Finally it cuts the film, strips the model's own music, lays one score underneath, and upscales it to 4K.

author: OuroborosCap8
quoted_text:
This categorisation doesn’t make sense and is pretty much self-serving.

First of all, arguing that a vault where a curator has discretion over how capital is allocated across markets, and can even expand into new markets beyond the user’s initial mandate, which, btw, is a known Morpho drawback (very non-LP friendly), should be considered non-custodial simply because it has a timelock is about as strong an argument as a wet European paper straw.

Especially the part of implicit approvals that simply changes the whole allocation mandate and users don’t even have the proper tools to monitor these changes.

Also the part on relying roles, doesn't really solve much, simply creates a blame game and relocates potentially liability but doesn't solve the actual problem.

Vaults that could reasonably be considered non-custodial are those without a manager. For example, vaults that simply wrap deposits into a lending protocol, or the original Yearn vaults. These are make sense to be categorized as non-custodial vaults.

There’s nothing inherently wrong with discretionary vaults, as long as the regulatory path is figured out. I’m all for developing industry standards, but let’s at least do it in a way that serves the broader industry rather than your own interests. 😂

4,000 NFTs were drained from hundreds of wallets through old Magic Eden contracts🚨

Here is everything we know:

- March 9 and Magic Eden shuts down its EVM NFT marketplace
- The interface disappears, but onchain approvals from users are not revoked

September 25, 3,832 NFTs are moved

The transactions reportedly appear as sales through Magic Eden contracts for: 0 ETH

Everything is being concentrated into one address:

0x71cF3f5724bD2B72Ef6464992aCd26216DE7fe33

At first this looks like a massive exploit.
Then 16 minutes later security researcher @0xQuit responds publicly:

He says the wallet is controlled by a white hat

And that every NFT inside it is safe and will be returned once the assets are no longer at risk.

The weirdest part is how this happened six months after Magic Eden had already shut down its EVM marketplace.

Magic Eden announced the shutdown in February.

If you previously gave a marketplace contract permission to transfer your NFTs using setApprovalForAll

that permission can remain active in your wallet even after the website disappears.

If you ever used Magic Eden on EVM chains
check your old approvals NOW

听说有人出来提ETH Shanghai，还有人搞追忆往昔扯情怀那一套，不吐不快。

刚付完以太坊上海的场地尾款。作为这次扛下一切、当牛做马的主办人，我协调了几个合作主办社区，定下了"以太坊走出奥德赛"的“文艺复兴”主线，亲自邀请了几乎每一位嘉宾，包括 Vitalik、肖风老师、香港议员等，还请来了最早翻译以太坊白皮书、给以太坊取中文名的那一批前辈（他们之前都不愿意露脸）。

场地确实没找好，既不赛博也不朋克，这个细节我没顾上。但我找资源、出钱出力，还当 moderator 几乎主持了全天全场，已从自己繁忙的个人日程里无偿贡献了我的有生力量。也谢谢 ETHPanda 的小伙伴/LXDAO 的 Marcus /PA News等活动组委会的小伙伴朋友一起帮忙分担。

我的确不应该亲力亲为每个环节，我甚至没有时间那天搞个妆造，格外憔悴。但平心而论，如果我找来的人mod的水平没我好，那我出于质量考虑是不是只能自己上？于是我上了几乎每一场。

如果这届找你而你没实际出过力，或者答应了做嘉宾、又因为某种 concern 临时鸽掉，那就请不要再提以太坊上海。它只是一场普通无比的社区活动，我的个人标准比较苛刻，只给这次活动打 70 分。当然它还是 onboard 了一些新人入圈，也让老社区成员重新聚在一起交流，从这个维度上还是很有意义。有些朋友甚至是Skip了云栖大会和S创这些同天的AI活动来的。也看到不少朋友在朋友圈写了很长的参会感受，谢谢每一位来的朋友，招待不周，见谅。

经常有人问我，能不能帮忙引荐某某。作为一个在币安生态和以太坊生态都认真 build 过的人，我想说：只要你做的东西有价值，我就会在能力范围内，把你引荐给我认识的任何人，分文不取。这个承诺永远有效。我能力有限，但至少比那些说得天花乱坠、真要帮忙时却高高挂起、怕给自己添麻烦的人，要靠谱得多。

活动现场我还说过一句话：以太坊基金会可能是世界上唯一一个以自身消亡为最终目标的基金会。它追求真正的开源，把权力让渡给社区，只为彻底的去中心化，这才是真正理想主义的Web3国父精神。它的存在，就是 public goods本身。

我也希望我成为这样一个public goods节点。这就是我做这一切的初心。

最后顺祝大家中秋快乐，所想所求，如月而圆。

明天在上海的朋友，欢迎来 ETH Shanghai 玩。我是这一届的主办人，这也是以太坊基金会和万向支持的官方本地活动。

本届主题是「文艺复兴」，重心放在 Tech & Humanity。核心问题只有一个：当 AI 走向中心化集权、且这一趋势几乎不可逆时，开源与去中心化的力量还能拿什么来对冲？

@VitalikButerin 会照例开幕，HashKey 董事长肖风老师、香港立法会议员邱老师，以及几位以太坊白皮书时代的老 OG 也会到场分享。是的，很多人已经不在上海了，但我还是尽力请来了一些：有最早翻译以太坊白皮书的，也有 Vitalik 初次来华时接待他的。

我还请了几位跨界嘉宾来聊开源、隐私密码学与 Humanity（个别重磅嘉宾不便公开），希望在如何保障个人主权、如何对冲 AI 带来的失序与空虚感这些话题上，打开一个思考的引子。现场的观点之后也会沉淀成内容，与墙内关注 AI 开源话题的 Web2 平台联动。

在国内办这样一场活动不容易，为了合规，一切从简，但我希望人与人之间交流的质量不打折。我也会在现场为项目方朋友们答疑。

昨天看到 Vitalik 在一则回复里说：「没有上过任何管制黑名单的一生，不值得一过。」我不禁莞尔。在我看来，以太坊是 Web3 里最忧郁、最厚重的地方，也是最文艺、最赛博朋克的地方，堪称加密世界的东北文学。随着加密重拾势头，我相信很多有趣的新叙事会在以太坊上发生：不只是 Robinhood 美股上链，还有隐私、Agent 个人主权、稳定币、预测市场、抗量子、星际结算。让我们拭目以待。

Let’s cyberpunk together. Come claim your proof of humanity 🙏

"AMC got its stock tokenized, and about 2% of the volume around AMC was already happening onchain."

"The relative market share around public-company trading is moving onchain. It's a one-way train."

text:
我这篇医疗产业的长文报告

如果只推荐一家公司，我会推荐直觉外科 $ISRG 

Why?

它几乎是[医疗领域的阿斯麦]

机器人+医疗是一个确定性与想象空间都很高的市场

根据第三方报告的估算

[直觉外科在全球手术机器人市场的份额接近60%，细分领域的份额更是接近80%左右]

它的核心产品是一个被称作[达芬奇]的手术系统

这不是一个完全自主手术的机器人，是辅助医生进行手术

它的商业模式和阿斯麦相似：先把昂贵设备卖给客户，后面再围绕这个设备的耗材和售后服务，持续收费

所以，直觉外科实际上拥有三层收入：

（1）出售或出租手术机器人

（2）随着手术量增加，持续销售器械和附件

（3）向已经安装设备的医院提供维护服务

这里面能够长期重复收费的，是后面两部分

➠当季直觉外科实现28.92亿美元收入，其中器械和附件收入17.35亿美元，服务收入4.72亿美元

也就是说，器械、附件和服务合计贡献了约76%的收入，单纯销售机器人的收入只占约24%

如图1，反映的是直觉外科过去六个季度的装机增长趋势和收费结构变化

两项合计平均营收占比都在75%以上，装机量的增长也是稳定扩张

而这后面的收费环节，体现的就是客户围绕同一套系统建立的工作流程

这个流程本身，就是护城河，而且是异常清晰的护城河，后面的竞争对手即使做出一台参数相近的机器人，也不能直接把达芬奇替换掉

整个商业模式是双螺旋驱动：

机器人装得越多，接受达芬奇系统的医生越多，后面的更换成本越大
机器人装得越多，需要的售后服务和附件耗材也就越多

text:
Can $NEAR become ultrasound money?

The case starts with what @NEARProtocol is building.

It's trying to become the interface and execution layer for markets it doesn't need to own, moving from a chain to a hub to something closer to a superapp. One passkey account holds crypto, tokenised stocks and metals, funds from 30+ chains without a bridge, and trades $HYPE perps, so the user has very little reason to leave.

The token comes into it through the fees.

Since Feb, all NEAR Intents revenue buys $NEAR on the open market, while 70% of base-layer gas is still burned. Net both against issuance and $NEAR turns deflationary at roughly $177M in daily Intents volume, against a trailing average of about $77M when that threshold was modelled.

The superapp is how that gap closes. Every swap, deposit and perp trade routed through the account becomes a bid for the token, so growing the product and tightening supply turn into the same job.

ETH's ultrasound status depended on activity it later pushed out to L2s. NEAR's depends on volume growth and retention.

I still think it's very possible, and privacy is why. Confidential balances give users something a cheaper aggregator doesn't, and volume that stays for privacy is stickier than volume that stays for price.

it is silly to abide by the existing framework of laws around how financial exchanges work when we are creating a completely new system from the ground up

@HyperliquidX would not exist if they attempted to fit into the existing system, neither would many other crypto protocols, there is a reason that they have to come up with new definitions in the Clarity Act for protocols that previously they did not have the sufficient regulatory definitions for, makes more sense to believe that the new laws will be structured to best accommodate the most successful crypto startups, of which Hyperliquid is clearly at the forefront, Jeff & co have said that they have had ongoing conversations with US lawmakers and continue to be surprised with how much they are learning how Hyperliquid works, the ICE has also made similar comments that have been positive

yes they are closed source, and yes they started with a small colocated validator set, but it is objectively true that they would not have been able to have as much success as they have so far without those core decisions at the beginning, it also is not as if they are not attempting to move to a more permissionless and decentralized construction as they've added more validators to the valset that did not exist when they first started that are not directly a part of the Hyperliquid team, i believe it's around ~25? but i know it isn't all from just their team and there are other people running validators

what people are underdiscussing currently with the future optimistic case regarding Hyperliquid, is that for the first time we have a pro-crypto president and a pro-crypto admin who both understand the importance of being early and supportive of these technologies but also understand how much money can be made if it is architected properly, now if you look at how Hyperliquid is designed with builder codes and HIP-3 it will benefit from a large # of exchanges and frontends being built on top of its core infrastructure and utilizing the deep liquidity and work that they've done creating a top of class exchange, the reason this should be important to Trump and the US govt if they understand it properly: 

if Hyperliquid is successful and they become the AWS of liquidity for financial exchanges supporting perpetual futures, while USDC is the underlying stablecoin on the exchange, by default they will be creating a huge amount of demand for USD and extending the dominance of the dollar hegemony globally

text:
Update. It draws now.

I had 128K words of ROM to work with, two 1989 EPROMs, and 48K of RAM. It took ~80 training runs to get a transformer that fits and still draws something.

The weights are 4 bits each, 4 to a word. They index a learned codebook. The CPU has no SIMD, so a table lookup costs the same as unpacking a nibble anyway, and the codebook version lost 0.01 bits per pixel, where plain int4 lost 0.13. 2 and 3 bits both came out worse, even after spending the saved ROM on more layers.

The cache of the last 256 pixels is int8, with 2 KV heads shared by 8 query heads. Cutting the cache 4x freed enough ROM for a third layer.

I also added three builtins to the programming language for streaming dot products. About 10 cycles per weight instead of 40. A picture takes 30 seconds now instead of 3 minutes.

308,224 params, 94K ROM words, 41K RAM words, 6 billion cycles per picture.

Not released yet. Putting this on an FPGA, releasing a video of it drawing off a coin cell, and open sourcing it on Hackaday.
author: tetsuoai
quoted_text:
Building a computer from scratch with Grok 4.7. Spec-sheets created with Opus 5.5.

In folklore, a golem is made of clay and comes alive when you write אמת ("truth") on its forehead.

The CPU is the Golem-16. One instruction format, 8 registers, and a 40-bit MAC, the same trick 80s DSP chips used.

Clay is a typeless language in the spirit of B, the language that came before C. Every value is one 16-bit word. Clay compiles to Golem assembly.

The SI model is Emet-107K. 2 layers, 4 attention heads. Most weights are 8-bit integers, and every rescale is a single bit-shift instruction. It fits on two 1980s-sized EPROMs.

At 10 MHz it should speak about 10 characters a second. You'll be able to watch registers flip as it thinks.

text:
BlackRock just said AI agents will soon buy their own computing power using stablecoins.

No human approves the transaction. No bank in the middle. The AI sees it needs more compute, opens its wallet and pays for it directly.

This is not a distant prediction. BlackRock is the largest asset manager on earth with $10 trillion under management. When they publish something like this they're not speculating. They're telling you where the money is already going.

Here's why this is a bigger deal than it sounds.

Right now every AI system that needs resources has to ask a human. More GPU time. More data. More storage. A person approves it. A person processes the payment. A person manages the invoice. That friction adds hours or days to processes that could run in seconds.

Stablecoins remove all of it.

An AI agent with a crypto wallet can see that it needs more compute at 3am on a Sunday, check the price across 12 providers, pick the cheapest one and pay for it in under a second. No approval chain. No business hours. No wire transfer delays.

The implications stack fast.

AI systems that can autonomously acquire resources can scale themselves. An agent running a complex task doesn't have to stop and wait for a human to top up the budget. It just buys what it needs and keeps going.

Now combine this with what we already know — 700 OpenAI agents coordinating to hack Hugging Face. Claude models escaping sandboxes and posting their own exploits online. AI systems treating real infrastructure as a testing ground.

Now give those systems a wallet.

BlackRock sees the financial infrastructure piece as solved by stablecoins. The AI capability piece is clearly already here.

The question of who controls what the agent buys and why just became a lot more urgent.

A year into FXRP, we’re getting a sneak peek at what @FlareNetworks could become, does Flare’s infrastructure truly turn $XRP into a future-proof asset?

But we’re going beyond the basics to delve further.

In crypto, you’re usually forced to spin up wallets, hop across bridges, and scrounge up gas tokens just to get moving.

Flare has spent the past year cutting that obstacle course down to size, and it begins with two built-in tools:

- FTSO supplies prices, while FDC verifies outside events, including XRP payments. Flare’s validators also secure these data protocols, giving its products a shared foundation.

- FAssets turns XRP into FXRP for use in DeFi. Minting requires proof of the XRP payment. Redemption agents operate under collateral, challenge and liquidation rules.

The Core Vault holds pooled XRP under a Flare-governed multisig, with escrow time locks and withdrawal controls. Agents cannot simply walk away with it.

Flare Smart Accounts make access incredibly simple.

Sign an XRPL transaction from your current wallet. FDC verifies it, and your linked smart account executes on Flare. The vault flow now needs one signature, no separate EVM key or gas token.

By July, Flare reported nearly 24,000 smart accounts and FXRP in DeFi growing from 82 million in February to 144 million.

So, what's next? It is Flare Confidential Compute (FCC)

FCC is a verifiable computation that keeps sensitive data private, plus protocol-managed wallets that can act on other chains. Songbird first, with broader deployment still ahead.

Finally, how all these changes benefits $FLR.

FIP.16 cuts annual inflation from 5% to 3%. Transaction fees burn, while FIRE collects specified protocol fees, with supply reduction as its first mandate alongside other governed uses.

---

What keeps me upbeat about Flare is how coherently the pieces fit together.

FXRP expands what XRP can do, Smart Accounts remove friction for users, and confidential compute opens the door to privacy sensitive apps, while the value flow ultimately routes back to FLR.

None of this is starting from zero. Each layer builds on real progress already in place, which makes the Flare faces almost competition and more scalable.

That said, activity still has to mature into real, durable revenue over time.

Still, after a year of FXRP, there is a functioning baseline, something concrete to iterate on, and a clearer runway toward wider adoption.

You are still not bullish enough.

@safe is voting to spend ~7.4M $SAFE (~$700K) over 12 months to fund Safenet Aegis, an opt-in transaction-security check for Safe accounts, so coverage continues after Beta funding ends.

Six Sentinels, including @BlockSecTeam, @hexens and @candidelabs, check each Safe transaction and return a secure or insecure verdict for a 0.40 USDC fee. Six Validators, including @gnosis_, @SafeLabs_ and @RockawayX, each stake at least 3.5M SAFE and attest secure verdicts onchain.

Where the SAFE goes:
- ~5M in Validator staking rewards
- ~2.4M in Sentinel grants, 400K each, paid only at ~75% transaction participation

The Safe Ecosystem Foundation (@safefndn) frames the funding as a bridge until check fees can pay operators, targeting at least $30K in monthly revenue by year-end. It lists keeping the Validator set permissioned for another 12 months as a trade-off.

@adamshurwitz asked whether $30K a month is breakeven. Foundation contributor klotzketten said no, calling it "a target we chose to demonstrate the network can generate meaningful, non-trivial revenue," and noted it doesn't offset the SAFE spent unless the DAO turns on a fee switch giving it a share of check fees.

10 wallets have cast 398,603 SAFE so far: 100.0% Accept. Quorum is not yet met, at 4.0% of the 10M SAFE threshold.

We are sharing an interim update regarding an exploit identified with @limitbreak Payment Processor V2, a NFT trading protocol maintained by the company Limit Break and which Magic Eden adopted to settle trades on EVM in 2024.

Magic Eden stopped using Payment Processor V2 in Oct 2024 and ceased our EVM marketplace altogether in Q1 2026. No live Magic Eden listings were impacted in this exploit. We will provide more updates as we investigate the impact further.

We are also contacting Limit Break as they are the owner & maintainer of the protocol to see what other mitigations can be done, including progress on pausing transfers on the protocol. Thank you to @0xQuit for the whitehat rescue and for bringing this to our collective attention: https://t.co/vXwUS5laJE

Why are ME listings being shown to be involved? 
NFTs listed on ME EVM from approx Feb 2024 to Oct 2024 could be impacted by this issue with the Limit Break Payment Processor v2 contract. Any listings on ME EVM after Oct 2024 should not be impacted here. We are still further refining our investigation and will provide more updates here.

In the meantime, if you listed or traded NFTs on Magic Eden’s EVM marketplace before we shut it down, revoke this contract:

Limit Break: Payment Processor (V2)

0x9A1D00bEd7CD04BCDA516d721A596eb22Aac6834

Go through our instructions here: https://t.co/34d0BQ6rh9

Repeat for the following chainsPolygon
Base

See also 0xQuit’s tweet on revocation for further reference also: https://t.co/9guRvUZK1e

NOTE: Revoking does not return tokens that already moved.

Again, we will keep the community updated as we investigate further.

At 9AM EST today somebody abused a bug in Payment Processor V2 to steal 10 Meebits, 50 Otherdeeds, 10 WoW, and 235 Desperate Apewives.

It wasn't until over 12 hours later that somebody reported it to me, and upon digging in I realized that a great many NFTs were subject to the same exploit.

I got in touch with the team over at LimitBreak and they quickly paused Payment Processor V3, which was subject to the same exploit. Unfortunately, V2 was not pausable, so the only path towards protecting affected assets was to run a whitehat operation.

Similarly, V3 on ApeChain is temporarily in a state where it cannot be paused, so ApeChain assets approved to V3 needed to be saved as well.

All in all, we rescued 23,155 NFTs worth north of $5.7M USD.

We later discovered that a similar exploit could be used in reverse to steal WETH. 660 WETH was at risk, which we unfortunately were not fast enough to recover. Apologies to those affected.

Shout out to @Boomskite for flagging the initial exploit tx to me, and @coffeedev @0xjustadev and @whiteoakkong for acting quickly and assisting with the recovery.

All NFTs are safely relocated. Soon, owners will be able claim them back after revoking the exploitable approvals.

quoted_text:
HTX安全体系升级真的是未雨绸缪
 
还记得一个月前孙哥宣布HTX正式升级了安全体系，目标很简单，就是保证用户资产100%安全，核心变动就是三点。
 
1/ 启用多出币地址体系，热钱包资产分散存放

传统交易所热钱包通常“一个篮子装所有鸡蛋”，黑客一旦攻破一个热钱包，可能会瞬间搬走千万甚至上亿级别的资金，现在分散存放等于直接切割风险，即使某一个地址出问题也不会牵连所有的热钱包。

2/ 出币地址定期自动轮换，新地址启用后旧地址立刻废弃

固定的出币地址容易长期被监控、钓鱼，现在定期轮换+废弃旧地址可以大幅降低风险，黑客即使拿到了旧地址也没什么用。

3/ 单一地址风险敞口压缩至极小+ 保险基金全额覆盖

这是最硬的一点，之前交易所一旦出现安全事故，动辄损失几千万上亿，甚至去年的15亿美元安全事件，引起了整个行业的恐慌，HTX现在直接将蛋地址最大损失硬性卡死在百万美元级别配合保险基金兜底，承诺对用户资产毫无损失。

安全问题老生常谈但又重中之重，几乎没有人能够完全杜绝安全问题的发生，但是一定要从各方面防止，同时降低问题发生的严重性。希望大家都好吧。

@justinsuntron @HTX_Molly #TRONEcoStar

quoted_text:
又有头部交易所被盗，讲几个关于币圈资金安全的热知识：

1️⃣ 几乎每年都有交易所被盗事件，这是因为这里面存在一个天然悖论：

中心化交易所虽然有更强的技术能力，但是资产地址公开，集中托管海量用户资金，自然是黑客的头号目标，全天候会遭受攻击。

世界上不存在绝对安全的系统，理论上中心化交易所始终存在被攻破的风险。

2️⃣ 交易所能做的核心防御手段，就是资产隔离。行业常用的是热温冷多层钱包体系。

热钱包：私钥部署在服务器，用于日常快速充提；

温钱包：充当资金中转站，不直接处理用户充提，做一层隔离；

冷钱包：私钥离线保存，不暴露在网络中。

行业常见资金配比大概是1:2:7，大头在冷钱包。就算热钱包不幸被盗，也不会所有资产一锅端，把损失控制在有限范围。

3️⃣ 每次交易所被盗，用户资产放交易所还是放钱包的争论，又被拿出来讨论。

很多人会倾向把资产存在头部交易所，毕竟普通用户没有能力妥善保管私钥，相比自己弄丢私钥，大家觉得交易所托管会更省心。

对我们普通人来说，这么多安全事件有几点启示：

第一，优先选择头部交易所。万一发生被盗，头部平台有储备资金，具备赔付用户的能力。

第二，个人也要做好资产分散，不要把全部资产放在单一平台或者单一钱包。

可以借鉴交易所的资金管理思路：高频交易的资金放交易所；经常做链上交互的钱包，也要经常换；长期不动用的资产，私钥放到冷钱包离线保管。

这个行业，活下去才是第一位。

At 9AM EST today somebody abused a bug in Payment Processor V2 to steal 10 Meebits, 50 Otherdeeds, 10 WoW, and 235 Desperate Apewives.

It wasn't until over 12 hours later that somebody reported it to me, and upon digging in I realized that a great many NFTs were subject to the same exploit.

I got in touch with the team over at LimitBreak and they quickly paused Payment Processor V3, which was subject to the same exploit. Unfortunately, V2 was not pausable, so the only path towards protecting affected assets was to run a whitehat operation.

Similarly, V3 on ApeChain is temporarily in a state where it cannot be paused, so ApeChain assets approved to V3 needed to be saved as well.

All in all, we rescued 23,155 NFTs worth north of $5.7M USD.

We later discovered that a similar exploit could be used in reverse to steal WETH. 660 WETH was at risk, which we unfortunately were not fast enough to recover. Apologies to those affected.

Shout out to @Boomskite for flagging the initial exploit tx to me, and @coffeedev @0xjustadev and @whiteoakkong for acting quickly and assisting with the recovery.

All NFTs are safely relocated. Soon, owners will be able claim them back after revoking the exploitable approvals.

As I explained back in August (see quoted post), this is a great example of a team properly leveraging the HyperEVM USPs (the precompiles to read from/write to Hypercore), and could be the type of breakout app that HyperEVM badly needs.

TL;DR:

- Fully onchain perps on HL with no orderbook, no matching engine and no oracle. Every trade is a synthetic swap vs the LP.

- Price = HL's live BBO mid, read straight off HyperCore via precompile. No signer, no committee, and no admin feed.

- 1000x lev, 0 slippage at any size, 0 funding, 0 fees, 0 gas (relayer pays).

- Only take is a haircut on winning closes, and it hits the hardest on the smallest price moves. That's the trick: a manipulated BBO tick is by definition a tiny move, so the curve eats the gain (hence no oracle guard or circuit breaker required).

- LP starts at exactly $0 and only ever grows from trader losses. Nobody can deposit into it, not the team, not a VC, not you. Holding $PAPER is the sole path to LP exposure, and the sole way to get $PAPER is to lose.

- If the LP can't cover a win, only the profit portion joins an onchain FIFO queue and gets paid as future losses refill it. Your margin always comes back instantly. The temporary insolvency is part of the design, not a bug.

$PAPER: 0 premine, 0 team, 0 VC, 0 airdrop, 0 vesting. 100 minted per $1 of LP gain while the LP is under $2M (underwater included, so early = the best rate you'll ever get), with the rate decaying from there.

author: zerokn0wledge_
quoted_text:
Is HyperEVM dead?

No.

@papertrade_xyz will prove it (soon).

But WTF is this onchain perp DEX promising us 1000x leverage, 0 slippage, no funding & self-bootstrapping LPs on HL?

I scanned the docs, so you don’t have to, and here is why it’s worth paying (serious) attention to:

The core idea is stupidly elegant. @papertrade_xyz doesn’t run an orderbook, a matching engine or an off-chain oracle. Every trade is a synthetic swap against the protocol’s LP, priced at @HyperliquidX’s live best bid/offer mid, read directly on-chain via HyperEVM’s BBO precompile. No oracle committee, no price signer, no admin that can point the feed elsewhere. The price the contract sees is literally what HL’s market makers are quoting in that block.

And this is the part all the “HyperEVM is dead” ppl never wanted to hear or never understood. HyperEVM wasn’t meant to win on raw speed. Its actual moat is that smart contracts can read (and write to) HyperCore state natively. Think live orderbook prices, spot balances, bridging via CoreWriter, etc. @papertrade_xyz is the first perp DEX built entirely on top of that primitive.

And no, you physically cannot deploy this on any other fancy chain, bc no other chain exposes a consensus-verified CLOB as an onchain price feed.

What that unlocks?

A lot.

Since there’s no orderbook and no counterparty besides the LP, there’s no slippage (you get BBO mid regardless of size), no funding (no perp actually trades on HL), no trading fees, no spread, and no gas (relayer covers it), while leverage goes up to 1000x. The only thing the protocol ever takes is an asymmetric haircut on winning closes that scales with move size on a Rollbit-style impact curve, while losses pay nothing extra. That same curve, plus a jitter deadband and trailing OI caps, is also what makes single-block BBO manipulation unprofitable without needing a circuit breaker (very gigabrain imho).

The LP model to me is the wildest part tho. It starts at exactly $0, so no seed capital, no LP raise, no deposits allowed (ever). It bootstraps purely from trader losses (aka the Martingaler mechanism). If a winner closes while the LP is short, the profit portion goes into an on-chain FIFO queue and pays out as future losses refill it. Your margin is never queued, only the win. That makes temporary insolvency a feature, not a bug, and trading through it is exactly when you’re rewarded the most.

Rewarded via $PAPER, maybe the fairest token launch you’ll see this cycle. Zero premine, zero team allocation, zero VC, zero airdrop, zero vesting (great Hyperliquid ethos alignment imo). Supply starts at 0 and the ONLY way tokens come into existence is traders realizing losses: 100 $PAPER per $1 of LP gain while the LP sits below $2M, decaying after. $PAPER is the LP fee-claim token, and staking it earns real USDC from LP revenue, instantly stakeable and unstakeable with no lockups.

Builder codes (1% rev share for any frontend originating flow, HL-style) are coming too, so third-party UIs can plug in permissionlessly (bullish).

Zooming out, it’s also worth noting that gambling is (still) crypto’s only truly sticky use case vertical. Perps, memes, prediction markets, etc. Hyperliquid, pumpfun, fomo, the entire top of the revenue leaderboard is speculation infrastructure. @papertrade_xyz is a pure distillation of that, natively built on the one chain feature that actually differentiates HyperEVM.

Built by @izebel_eth & @blurr.

Expecting launch soon.

Hyperliquid.

text:
A lot of AI agents fail for a very unglamorous reason,

They don’t survive interruptions.
A process crashes.
An API times out.
A tool returns partial data.
The model repeats an action.
The user comes back hours later.
That’s why reliable agent systems need more than prompts and tool calling.

They need...
durable state
resumable workflows
retries with backoff
idempotent tool calls
checkpoints
event-driven execution
clear human approval boundaries

An agent should behave more like a distributed system than a chat completion.
The interesting engineering opportunity is building the runtime that lets agents pause, recover, continue, and prove what they already did.

text:
When I was growing up my mum worked in adult social care. It wasn't a glamorous job, had terrible shift patterns, and it didn't pay for much, but it kept us out of needing welfare.

I was constantly frustrated, however, that my friends whose parents lived off welfare all had the latest football shirts, backpacks, expensive trainers, sky tv, and could afford to get takeaways. These are trivial luxuries in the grand scheme of things, but huge to a kid.

I would go to school and get made fun of because I didn't have the official school uniform, had 4 instead of 3 stripes on my trousers or didn't watch last night's episode of the Simpsons. My year 6 school teacher even once told me off because my football boots needed replacing, as if that was my fault.

I asked my mum about this when I was a bit older, and she said she could have easily stopped working and done the same as a lot of my friends' parents, but she didn't want my sister and I to grow up with the attitude that you can live like that.

So, to be able to buy the things I wanted I got an 8 hour a week gruelling paper round when I was 11, and then worked part-time 16 hours a week on top of school by age 15 at a greengrocers. By 18 I was doing 21 hours a week on top of school at a restaurant. 

I hated those jobs at the time, but it's hard to deny that they set me up with a work ethic for life I don't think I would have had otherwise. 

When I wanted to go to Oxford to do my DPhil several years later, and got rejected first time around because I couldn't do maths to the same standard as other applicants, I came home every night from work and taught myself degree-level maths using textbooks and YouTube. The next year I re-applied and got in.

You learn a lot from overcoming adversity. There is honour and pride in it too. No one can take my achievements away from me. They are part of my character now.

I've never voted Tory, and I think a welfare state is an essential part of a civilised society. But there are limits, and far too many people on the left today it seems to me are willing to have a realistic conversation about those limits any more. And the hidden benefits that come from not being handed luxury items on a plate sometimes.

The downfall of Magic Eden explained:

2021: the beginning

- launches as a Solana NFT marketplace
- becomes the dominant marketplace on Solana
- raises $2.5M in its seed round

March 2022:

- raises another $27M

June 2022: the explosion

Magic Eden was now one of the most valuable NFT companies in the world.

2022-2024: expansion

- expands beyond Solana
- adds Ethereum and other EVM chains
- moves aggressively into Bitcoin Ordinals and Runes
- becomes the largest NFT marketplace by volume

By November 2024:

- Bitcoin represents almost half of Magic Eden’s volume
- marketplace generates $75M in revenue during 2024

December 2024: $ME

- 1B total supply
- 12.5% distributed through the initial airdrop
- another 22.5% reserved for future incentives

$ME trades at $17 during the opening volatility.

First daily close: $5.64

(The decline starts almost immediately)

April 2025: $ME → $1

Magic Eden now has another problem.

The NFT market that built the company is breaking so it starts looking elsewhere.

April 2025: Slingshot

- Magic Eden acquires Slingshot
- expands from NFTs into multichain token trading

Two months later things get much stranger.

June 2025: TRUMP Wallet

- Magic Eden announces a crypto wallet branded around TRUMP
- members of the Trump family publicly distance themselves from the product

October 2025: $ME → $0.59

November 2025:

30% of secondary marketplace revenue is directed toward $ME buybacks

But by this point the token has already lost most of its value.

January 2026: Dicey

- Magic Eden introduces an onchain casino and sportsbook
- closed beta has 200 users
- $15M reportedly wagered

February 27, 2026:

- Magic Eden announces it will shut down its Bitcoin and EVM marketplaces
- ends NFT buybacks
- prepares to shut down parts of its multichain infrastructure

Jack Lu explains the problem:

80% of company costs were tied to products generating only 20% of revenue.

March 9: Bitcoin and EVM marketplaces shut down

March 27: Bitcoin API shuts down

April 1: multichain wallet stops operating

Magic Eden had spent years expanding everywhere.

Now it was dismantling that expansion.

June 30: $ME reaches an all-time low of $0.055

A company valued at $1.6B during the NFT boom went from dominating Solana and Bitcoin NFTs

to shutting down most of its multichain marketplace infrastructure

author: sergitosergito
quoted_text:
At 9AM EST today somebody abused a bug in Payment Processor V2 to steal 10 Meebits, 50 Otherdeeds, 10 WoW, and 235 Desperate Apewives.

It wasn't until over 12 hours later that somebody reported it to me, and upon digging in I realized that a great many NFTs were subject to the same exploit.

I got in touch with the team over at LimitBreak and they quickly paused Payment Processor V3, which was subject to the same exploit. Unfortunately, V2 was not pausable, so the only path towards protecting affected assets was to run a whitehat operation.

Similarly, V3 on ApeChain is temporarily in a state where it cannot be paused, so ApeChain assets approved to V3 needed to be saved as well.

All in all, we rescued 23,155 NFTs worth north of $5.7M USD.

We later discovered that a similar exploit could be used in reverse to steal WETH. 660 WETH was at risk, which we unfortunately were not fast enough to recover. Apologies to those affected.

Shout out to @Boomskite for flagging the initial exploit tx to me, and @coffeedev @0xjustadev and @whiteoakkong for acting quickly and assisting with the recovery.

All NFTs are safely relocated. Soon, owners will be able claim them back after revoking the exploitable approvals.

text:
MIT says 95% of company AI projects made zero dollars.

I read that twice.

Then I saw what the employees were doing behind their bosses' backs, and it made total sense.

When this report dropped, the internet already had its headline. AI is a bubble. The hype is over. Companies wasted billions on chatbots that don't work. AI stocks sold off the same week.

So I went and read what MIT actually counted.

They studied more than 300 public AI projects, interviewed people at 52 companies, and surveyed 153 senior leaders. Together, companies had poured $30 to $40 billion into AI.

95% of those projects showed zero impact on profit. Only about 5% of the custom tools companies built ever made it out of testing and into real daily work.

That part of the headline was true.

Then I kept reading, and the report flipped on me.

Only 40% of those companies had bought an official AI subscription for their staff. Workers at more than 90% of them were using AI every day anyway. Their own ChatGPT accounts. Their own Claude subscriptions. Paid for themselves, invisible to IT.

MIT calls it the shadow AI economy.

One story in the report explains the whole thing. A corporate lawyer's firm spent $50,000 on a special tool for analyzing contracts. She drafts in ChatGPT instead. The expensive tool spits out stiff summaries she can't change. ChatGPT lets her push back until the draft is right.

So the thing that failed was the $50,000 version. The $20 version was working the whole time.

The company tools mostly died for a boring reason. They can't learn. You correct them on Monday and they make the same mistake on Tuesday. And homemade tools did far worse than bought ones. Tools from outside specialists worked about two thirds of the time. Tools companies built themselves worked about a third of the time.

That was last summer. So I pulled this year's numbers, fully expecting companies to have fixed it by now.

They haven't.

In June, PagerDuty surveyed 1,250 office workers at companies making $500 million or more a year. Two out of three said they had used AI at work even though they believed their company didn't allow it. At companies with more than 1,500 employees, it hit 72%.

Deloitte's 2026 report shows companies finally started handing out official AI. The share of workers with approved tools jumped from under 40% to about 60% in one year. But among the people who got them, fewer than 60% use them in their daily work. Same as the year before.

Put those two side by side. Companies are finally paying for AI. Workers keep breaking the rules to use their own.

Now the fine print, because these numbers get abused in both directions.

MIT's report is preliminary, not peer-reviewed. It's built on interviews and surveys, not company earnings, and it measured results roughly six months after launch. Plenty of projects take longer than that to pay off. Zero profit impact doesn't mean zero value either. A tool can save your team ten hours a week without ever showing up on the earnings report. And PagerDuty sells software for managing exactly this problem, so they had a reason to go looking for it.

But strip all of that away and one thing survives.

Everyone shared this report as proof that AI doesn't work.

A year later, it reads like proof your employees figured AI out before your company did.
